title: Keeping Up with Science: A 42-Year-Old Childhood Obesity Theory May Be Wrong (B2)

elements.content: Welcome to Keeping Up with Science. Review the research context and metadata below:

Session Overview:
• Duration: 60 minutes
• Languages: 🇬🇧 English
• Level: Upper-Intermediate (B2)
• Theme: Metabolism & Public Health Science

What is your initial reaction when reading about this scientific study?
How might this discovery change how we understand daily health or technology?
Master the core scientific vocabulary and collocations for this topic (10 items):

items.definition: a formal idea or set of ideas intended to explain something.
items.example: Scientists are re-examining a 42-year-old childhood obesity theory.

items.definition: the chemical processes that occur within a living organism in order to maintain life.
items.example: Basal metabolism accounts for most daily energy expenditure.

items.definition: a proposed explanation made on the basis of limited evidence.
items.example: The initial hypothesis was disproved by modern metabolic tracking.

items.definition: the action of spending or using up energy.
items.example: Daily energy expenditure varies significantly across age groups.

items.definition: a mutual relationship or connection between two or more things.
items.example: A statistical correlation does not prove a direct causal link.

items.definition: the fact or condition of being widespread.
items.example: The prevalence of childhood health conditions prompted extensive research.

items.definition: relating to heat or energy value of food.
items.example: Caloric balance depends on both diet and physical activity.

items.definition: the process of assessing something again.
items.example: Scientific progress relies on constant re-evaluation of old models.

items.definition: tending to spend much time seated; somewhat inactive.
items.example: A sedentary lifestyle contributes to energy imbalance.

items.definition: involving information about the same subjects over a long period of time.
items.example: Longitudinal studies provide robust evidence across decades.

elements.title: Grammar Explanation (Upper-Intermediate (B2))
elements.content:
Use modal + have + past participle to speculate about past scientific assumptions (e.g., Earlier researchers might have overlooked key metabolic variables).
🧩 Interactive Word Bank:
Tap a word chip below, then tap any empty bracket [_____] to place it!
might have
could have
past participle
past speculation
📝 Task 1 : Part A: Rule Formulation:
Complete the rule: Speculate on past possibilities with modal verb + have + _____.
📝 Task 1 : Part B: Structured Practice:
Researchers _____ underestimated basal metabolism.
Earlier studies _____ relied on imperfect tracking methods.
Scientists _____ drawn flawed conclusions from limited sample sizes.
Check Answers
Reset Board
🗣️ Task 2 : Interactive Speaking:
Speculate on why a long-standing scientific theory might have gone unchallenged for over four decades.
A comparative reflection on our habits and self-perceptions.
Analyze the core scientific findings and discuss the personal prompts in pairs:

prompts: Why must a long-standing scientific theory be re-evaluated when new evidence emerges?
How does human basal metabolism adapt during periods of intense physical growth?
What evidence is needed to transform a scientific hypothesis into established consensus?
How does daily caloric expenditure vary between active children and adults?
Why does confusing statistical correlation with direct causation lead to flawed health advice?
What factors explain the growing prevalence of childhood metabolic disorders worldwide?
How do ultra-processed foods affect total caloric intake and appetite regulation?
Why is a critical re-evaluation of public health guidelines necessary every decade?
How damaging is a prolonged sedentary lifestyle for growing children?
What insights can a longitudinal medical study provide that short trials cannot?

elements.placeholder: Record your partner's key arguments or shared hypotheses...

pairs.correct: They might have overlooked the data.
pairs.note: Past speculation modal structure: 'might have' + past participle.
